title: Given an array of numbers and a value K, you may remove up to K elements. Maximize the number of distinct elements remaining. Explain how a frequency count and a min-heap of the duplicate counts guide which removals help most.
shortTitle: Maximum Distinct Elements (Maximize Distinct Values After K Removals)
keyPoints: Numbers appearing exactly once are already distinct and cost zero removals.
For numbers appearing more than once, the surplus to remove is count minus one.
A min-heap of surplus counts lets you clear the cheapest duplicates first.
The greedy strategy spends the removal budget on the smallest surpluses to maximize conversions.
If budget remains after all duplicates are cleared, each further removal destroys one distinct element.
Time complexity is O(N + D log D) where D is the number of distinct values.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies, keep singles for free, then spend K removals clearing the smallest surplus counts first via a min-heap.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Maximum Distinct Elements** is a greedy Top K Elements problem.
- Numbers with frequency **exactly one** are already distinct and cost nothing.
- For numbers with frequency greater than one, the cost to make them distinct is `count - 1` removals.
- A **min-heap** of surplus counts lets you clear the cheapest duplicates first.
- After all duplicates are cleared, any remaining budget **removes distinct elements**, decreasing the count.
- Time is **O(N + D log D)** and space is **O(D)** where D is the number of distinct values.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a merchant category report has many duplicate codes. The compliance team may delete up to K entries to maximize how many categories appear exactly once for a clean audit. Categories already appearing once are free wins. For the rest, they clear the duplicates needing the fewest deletions first, because those convert to distinct most cheaply.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Distinct Elements asks you to maximize how many values appear exactly once after removing up to K elements, and it is a greedy problem with a clean two-phase structure. In the first phase, you count frequencies and separate the already-distinct values (frequency 1) from the duplicated values. You put the duplicate counts into a min-heap and spend your removal budget on the smallest surpluses first, because clearing a small surplus converts a value to distinct for the fewest removals.

In the second phase, if any budget remains after all duplicates have been cleared, each remaining removal must target an already-distinct element, reducing the count. This second phase is easy to miss but critical for correctness.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to clean a merchant category report for compliance. The report had many duplicate category codes, and the team could delete up to K entries to maximize how many categories appeared exactly once for a clean audit. The min-heap ensured the cheapest conversions happened first, and the two-phase structure handled the case where the budget exceeded the total surplus.

The senior-level insight is the greedy argument: per unit of budget, clearing the smallest surplus produces the highest return, and the exchange argument proves that any other ordering either matches or underperforms. Recognizing the two-phase structure and the greedy justification is what shows an interviewer you reason about the budget optimally.

Remember one sentence: spend removals on the smallest surplus counts first via a min-heap, then subtract any leftover budget from the distinct count.
